claim.quote: Discovery of a Narrow Resonance in ... Annihilation

date.note: Phys. Rev. Lett. 33, 1406. The discovery weekend at SPEAR was in November 1974 (CERN Courier); the publication date is used as the result date.

key_value_text.quote: at a center-of-mass energy of 3.105 ... 0.003 GeV. The upper limit to the full width at half-maximum is 1.3 MeV.
key_value_text.value: Peak at 3.105 ± 0.003 GeV; full width at half-maximum below 1.3 MeV

name: Discovery of a Narrow Resonance in e+e− Annihilation
notes: The paper title says "Discovery", so result_type is discovery; no sigma is quoted and the significance field says so.
The same resonance was found simultaneously at Brookhaven by S. Ting's group (fixed target); that experiment is not part of this record.

significance.quote: We have observed a very sharp peak in the cross section
significance.value: No statistical significance is quoted; the abstract reports a very sharp peak (observed) with a full width at half-maximum limit of 1.3 MeV

summary.plain: In November 1974 the Mark I experiment at SLAC's SPEAR ring found a very sharp peak in electron-positron collisions at a total energy of 3.105 GeV. The same particle, called J by Samuel Ting's Brookhaven group, was found independently. It was the first sign of the charm quark.
summary.technical: Mark I: a very sharp peak in the cross section for e⁺e⁻ → hadrons, e⁺e⁻ and possibly μ⁺μ⁻ at a centre-of-mass energy of 3.105 ± 0.003 GeV, with an upper limit of 1.3 MeV on its full width at half-maximum (Phys. Rev. Lett. 33, 1406, 2 December 1974). The resonance, called ψ at SLAC and J at Brookhaven, is the bound state of a charm quark and its antiquark.

title: Discovery of a Narrow Resonance in e+e− Annihilation
why_it_matters: SLAC's own history says the discovery of this new quark (charm) served as convincing evidence that the quark substructure of matter was valid; Burton Richter shared the 1976 Nobel Prize in Physics for it with Samuel Ting.
